name: Nell Sorensen
equipment: Heavy coat: a long suede coat with a sheepskin collar, very 1971
Pocket revolver: a little .32 her stage partner insisted she carry on the road, in her handbag
A set of mentalist's tricks: a thumb writer, a pack of marked cards, a pencil-lead nail
A handbill: MADAME NELL — THE MIND OF THE NORTH — NIGHTLY AT THE DUNES LOUNGE, ATLANTIC CITY
A good dress, and stage makeup in a tackle box
Hand mirror, in the makeup box
Opal's letter, inviting her back for the closing
Car: a rented 1976 Ford Pinto, green
features: Been Here Before (Survivor origin: advantage on initiative; when a fight or a fright begins she always knows the nearest way out of the room (the GM says); once per long rest she can reroll a failed saving throw, including a fear check, and must use the new roll; the first time each scenario she meets a horror like the one she survived (something on the water in the shape of a person she knew, Lantern Night 1962), the GM tells her one way it is the same)

The Thin Place (Sensitive: she knows when a presence is within 60 ft, though not where or what; she feels cold spots and the strongest emotion soaked into a room; once per scene she can open herself to the place and the GM gives her one true impression, at the cost of 1 Dread with no save; it is never control and never magic)

Read the Room (Sensitive: advantage on Insight checks to tell what a person is feeling, and she knows without a check when someone she is speaking with is frightened, grieving or hiding something, though not what)

Closer to the Edge (Sensitive, 2nd level: Dread from The Thin Place can't take her past 5; at Dread 3 or higher The Thin Place gives two impressions, and she can sense where a presence within 60 ft is, to within 10 ft)
Gift: Listener (Sensitive, 3rd level: her impressions often come as voices; once per scene she can hear the last words spoken in a place where someone died, as the GM chooses to give them)

The Séance Trade (Medium background: she reads people for a living on a stage; performers, spiritualist circles and grieving families welcome her; she knows every trick of the trade, which is how she knows when something is not a trick)

personality.traits: I talk fast and laugh loud and touch people's arms. On stage I am Madame Nell; off it I am a schoolteacher's daughter from Racine who chews her nails. I always know where the exits are.
personality.ideals: Everybody wants to be told the truth about the people they lost. I give them a kind version. Somebody should give them the real one.
personality.bonds: Pinecrest, where I was happy two summers. Opal, who wrote to me every Christmas for fifteen years and never once asked why I left. Curtis Seeley, who taught me to paddle a canoe and whom I have not let myself think about since 1962.
personality.flaws: I ran once, the morning after. I have never stopped being ashamed of it, and I am afraid that if I see it again, I will run again.

appearance: Thirty-six, small and quick, dark red hair under a silk head scarf she wears because it sells tickets, big hoop earrings, a long suede coat, very good at looking straight into your eyes.
backstory: Nell Sorensen was the drama counselor at Pinecrest in 1961 and 1962, twenty and twenty-one, fresh out of a Milwaukee teachers' college and stage-struck: she directed the Saturday revues and played every comic maid. On Lantern Night 1962, with no masks, she stood near the end of the dock beside Curtis Seeley, the waterfront director, who had been teaching her to paddle all summer, and watched him lean out over the water. His reflection did not move when he did. At midnight, from the Lodge window, she saw Curtis standing on the end of the dock in the rain, while Curtis's canoe light was out in the middle of the lake. She packed in the dark and caught the first bus from Larkin Corners in the morning, and never told anyone why. She has made her living since as a stage mentalist, MADAME NELL, THE MIND OF THE NORTH, in Catskills hotels and Atlantic City lounges: cold reading, a few honest tricks and, now and then, something she cannot explain and never puts in the act. Opal's letter about the closing came in August. She has been drinking more since. (Hook: 1962. She is the only living witness to the first double, and the GM should let it come back to her.)
